messages.content: what does i have been reading all morning tell you?
reading has been part of your morning for some time. it does not by itself say that you finished the book or that you read every moment without a break.
can you make a short conversation with that sentence?
what have you been doing? i have been reading all morning. did you finish the book? not yet. i stopped for tea, and i still have more to read.
why is not yet okay with all morning?
you can spend a whole morning reading and still have pages left. the time spent and the work left are different details.
say it simply.
you can spend a whole morning reading and still have pages left. the sentence gives time, rather than the end of the book.
now say it about yesterday.
i was reading all morning yesterday.
did that say whether i finished the book?
no. it says when you were reading, rather than whether you got to the end of the book.
make a short story using had already left. i want the order to be clear.

a woman calls her brother to ask whether he can bring a book from home. he says he had already left before the call. the book is still on his desk, so he cannot bring it on that journey. she says they can choose another day for the book. they still meet for lunch as they wanted.
keep the last sentence simple.
they still meet for lunch.
which came first, leaving home or the call?
he left home first. had already left puts that part before the call in the story.
can you change it so she calls before he leaves?
a woman calls her brother before he leaves home and asks him to bring a book from his desk. he takes it with him, and they meet for lunch.
why could he bring it in the changed story?
he was still at home when she asked, so the book was there for him to take. the changed order made a different choice possible.
can we say he would always bring a book when asked?
no. the story gives one example. another day could have different details, and he might not have a way to bring it.
if i say my sister could have moved the cup, does that say she did move it?
no. could have gives a possible explanation. it does not make that explanation a known fact.
i know she was in the room. is that enough?
she was there, so moving it was possible. you still do not know that she did it.
say it simply.
being in the room does not tell us that she moved the cup.
what should i ask her?
do you know where the cup went? it was on the desk before.
why not ask why did you move it?
why did you move it says she moved it before she has answered. asking what she knows keeps open what happened.
answer simply.
why did you move it says she moved it before she has answered. do you know where it went asks without choosing what happened.
my grandfather says he used to read near the window. does that mean he never reads there now?
used to is about a place where he read before. it does not tell you every detail about what he does now.
answer simply.
he read there before. ask whether he still reads there now.
write a question i could ask him.
do you still read near that window sometimes?
he says he now likes the chair near the door better. write a short reply asking why.
what do you like about that chair now?
he says he can see when people come in. can i write that he no longer likes the window?
not from that detail alone. he gave a reason for his new choice, but did not say he no longer likes the window at all.
can he like both places and still choose one more often?
yes. he can like both places and still choose the chair by the door most days.
say it simply.
he can like both places and choose one more often.
i need a note for my desk. i am leaving the room for a meeting, but i do not know what time i will return.
you could write: i am at a meeting and do not know my return time yet. please leave a message if you need me.
can you make it shorter without choosing a time?
i am at a meeting. please leave a message, and i will read it when i return.
does that say i will answer every message as soon as i am back?
no. reading a message and answering it are different things. the note does not say every answer will be ready right away.
say it simply.
no. the note says you will read it when you return. it does not say when you will answer.
now i know i will return after lunch. change the note.
i will return after lunch. please leave a message if you need me.
should i keep the line saying i do not know the return time?
not if the new information is clear. you can change the note to use what you know now, rather than leave two different messages about the same return.
i want a conversation where two people have breakfast together but choose different food. keep it simple.
what would you like? bread and cheese, please. i am having rice today. would you like some too? no, thank you. bread is enough for me. shall we sit by the window? yes, i would like that.
say my request simply.
write a simple conversation where two people have breakfast together but choose different food.
can both enjoy the time together without eating the same meal?
yes. sitting at a table together does not mean choosing the same food. each person can have what they want while still having a good conversation.
use sitting in a simple answer.
sitting together does not mean eating the same food. they can enjoy the conversation while each has a different meal.
now add that they both want tea.
would you like tea with your breakfast? yes, please. i would like tea too. then i will bring two cups.
did tea change their food choices?
no. they still chose bread and cheese for one person and rice for the other. tea is something they both want with those meals.
write a story about a child making up a game and then finding a rule that needs to be more clear.

a child puts three objects on a table and says that everyone should choose one. her brother takes one away and keeps it in his hand. she says he should have left it on the table, but he asks where that part of the rule was. she thinks, then says the rule again with more detail: choose one object by putting your hand near it, but do not take it away. they try again, and this time both understand what to do.
ask my request with clear.
write a story about a child making a game and learning that the rule needs to be more clear.
was the brother wrong to ask about the rule?
no. asking helped them find a detail that was not said. the child had one idea in mind, but the words did not yet give the whole idea.
what could she ask before saying the rule is ready?
can you tell me what you think the rule asks you to do?
why is that useful?
it can show whether another person got the same idea from the words. if not, they can work on the explanation before playing more.
does more clear always mean more words?
no. sometimes a few specific words help more than a long explanation. the goal is for the other person to understand the needed detail.
i have a pair of cups on the table. does that tell you their size?
a pair gives a number of two. it does not give their size, color, or whose they are.
say it simply.
there are two cups. the other details are not given.
can one cup be large and the other small?
yes. you can talk about two cups together even when they are not the same size. context can help show whether they were made to be used together.
keep just the simple example.
there are two cups: one large and one small.
what if i give the small one to my friend?
then one cup is with your friend and one is still with you, unless you also move the other. the two cups have not become one just because they are apart.
write a sentence that says they are in different places now.
one cup is on my table, and the other is with my friend.
does that tell us the small cup is now theirs?
no. they may only be using it. you need more information to know whose it is.
answer simply.
no. they could be using a cup that is not theirs.
can i thank someone for listening even if they have a different idea from mine?
yes. someone can listen and understand your words without choosing the same answer as you.
say it simply.
yes. listening does not mean choosing the same idea.
write a short thank you for that.
thank you for listening. we have different ideas, but i am happy we could talk.
use happy and different ideas in the message.
thank you for listening. we have different ideas, but i am happy we could talk.
does that say i changed my mind?
no. it says you are happy about the conversation, rather than saying you changed your idea.
explain simply.
no. you can be happy about talking while keeping your own idea.
can i ask them to tell me more about theirs?
yes. you could add: i would like to understand your idea better. could you tell me more about it?
write a story about one visit to a village and another visit later. show the different weather through details a child sees.

a child visits a village with her aunt. on the first visit, people sit outside with cups of tea, and the child sees flowers near the library. on the next visit, people have warm garments on, and snow is on the road. the same worker stands at the shop door and says hello. the child asks if it is the same place. her aunt says yes. some things changed with the weather, while some things stayed the same.
say my request simply.
write about a child going to the same village on different days, with different weather.
make it simple.
write about one visit to a village and another later, with different weather.
use one visit and another in a short request.
write about one visit to a village and another visit later, with different weather.
does the snow tell us what every village is like?
no. it is a detail of that village on that visit. other places or days can have different weather.
which person stayed the same in the story?
the worker at the shop door was there on both visits.
use both days in a simple answer.
the worker at the shop door was there on both days.
i read a story where a man goes to a shop. then i ask whether he bought bread. does the question add bread to the story?
no. it asks about something you do not know. unless the story gives an answer, the question does not add a new fact.
answer simply.
no. asking about bread does not say he bought it. we need the story to give that detail.
what if i say i want the made up next part to have him buy bread?
then we can add it as new story writing: he goes inside, buys bread, and carries it home. that is a chosen next part, rather than something we learned from the first question.
say it simply.
then buying bread can be part of the new story you asked us to make. it was not a fact given by your first question.
can you write the whole short story with that new part?
a man goes to a shop, buys bread, and carries it home. his daughter asks whether they can have some with lunch, and he says yes.
does that say the daughter was at the shop too?
no. she asks after he brings the bread home. we do not know where she was before.
answer simply.
no. her place before that was not given.
picoboi, change i might visit to i will visit. how does the meaning change?
might leaves the visit open. will makes it sound more sure, as a plan for what you are going to do.
explain simply.
might says it is possible. will says it more as a plan.
if i ask for that change in a writing example, do you know i really chose to visit?
no. changing a sentence for an example does not give a real fact about your plan. you would need to say that it is what you have chosen.
write two short example messages using the difference.
i might visit tomorrow if i have time. i will visit tomorrow after lunch.
why did the message with will add after lunch?
that was a new detail for the example. if you want only the word change, keep the same other words: i might visit tomorrow. i will visit tomorrow.
make my question simple.
why did the message with will add after lunch?
now do only the word change in i might visit my aunt.
i will visit my aunt.
